transcript.note: Round 1 — I built the incidence list by hand and classified every vertex by its lock state: a V edge locks the column, an H edge locks the row, so a vertex carrying both is untouchable (40, 23, 24, 13, 15, 44). Everything else I worked outward from the leaves and degree-2 chain points, because there the 360-degree winding test only has to hold at the *neighbour*. Concrete reasoning per group: (a) leaves and chain ends that only need to meet their single partner's row or column — 46 to (56,23) makes 22-46 horizontal in 2 cells, 9 slides along its locked column 43 to row 42 so 9-25 goes horizontal, 50 slides along its locked column 14 up to row 56 so 50-49 goes horizontal, 37 goes to (27,11) rather than the 1-cell (29,12) because (29,12) would sweep 37's bearing past neighbour 2's at 18 and be rejected on winding. (b) The hub 20 is locked to row 17 by 45-20, so I slid it *along* that row to column 27, which is 18's column: that turns 18-20 vertical and simultaneously makes 23-20 an exact 45 (dx=dy=6); 0 follows to (24,14) to keep 0-20 at 45. All four of 20's edges are then aligned. (c) 58 to (33,33) buys two segments at once — column 33 is 44's column and row 33 is 24's row — and 36 to (29,30) buys 36-44 horizontal while preserving the 45-36 diagonal (dx=dy=13). (d) 12 is locked to row 23 by two H edges, so I slid it along the row to column 43 (40's column) for 40-12 vertical; that costs the 38-12 diagonal, but the score is lexicographic with HV as primary key, so a segment upgrade beats a diagonal. 38 then starts a two-step walk to (33,18) where it will be vertical to 23 and 45 to 18. (e) 16 to (22,40) reaches 15's row; column 16 is unavailable because the existing 15-33 vertical edge already occupies it and dropping 16 on it would swallow a vertex. (f) 35 to (16,11) reaches 45's column, and 4 to (10,5) then sits at exactly dx=dy=6 from it while staying on row 5 for the 4-47 horizontal I set up next round. (g) Everything else is the first half of a two-round walk that is too long for one short move: 47 toward (3,5), 7 toward (0,40), 28 toward (14,49), 34 toward (57,27), 53 toward (48,15), 42 toward (19,42), and 33/43 converging on the shared row 22.

Round 2 — this closes the eight walks that were too long for a single short move last round, each one landing exactly on its partner's locked row or column. 38 finishes at (33,18): column 33 is 23's column, so 38-23 becomes vertical, and (33,18) is simultaneously dx=dy=6 from 18, so 38-18 upgrades to 45 in the same step; I checked that rows 18-23 of column 33 are empty so the new vertical edge does not swallow 44 or 58. 47 to (3,5) puts it on 4's row for the 4-47 horizontal while keeping the 47-8 vertical on column 3. 7 to (0,40) reaches 11's row while staying on column 0 for 7-48. 28 to (14,49) reaches 51's column, upgrading the 28-51 diagonal to a true vertical while 27-28 stays horizontal on row 49 — an upgrade from 45 to H/V is worth taking because HV is the primary key. 34 to (57,27) reaches 55's column while staying on 17's row. 53 to (48,15) reaches 22's column while staying on 54's row. 42 to (19,42) reaches 39's row. 33 to (16,22) meets 43 on row 22 — I moved the two toward each other rather than dragging one 7 cells, and 33 stays on column 16 so both of its existing verticals survive. Every one of these keeps the mover on the axis it was already locked to, which is why none of them can cost an existing segment.

Round 3 — the 2-18 segment looked dead because 18 is pinned to column 27 by two vertical edges (to 37 and to 20) and 2 is pinned to row 9, so the only meeting point is (27,9); but sliding 18 down to row 9 would leave leaf 37 at (27,11) sitting *inside* the 18-20 vertical span and get swallowed. The fix is to move the obstruction first: 37 drops to (27,7), below 18, so the two verticals leave 18 in opposite directions and 18 can take row 9. That is a real horizontal segment bought by relocating a leaf. It costs the 38-18 45, so I pay it back in the same round by sliding 38 up its own locked column 33 to row 15, which is exactly dx=dy=6 from the new 18 — column 33 rows 15-23 are empty, so the 38-23 vertical is unharmed. Separately I started the long slide of 16 east along its locked row 40: the target is column 33, which is simultaneously 58's column and, with 39 nudged one cell to (33,42), 39's column — so one destination buys two vertical segments. I checked the bearing of 58 and of 33 as seen from 16 at every intermediate column (22, 25, 28, 31, 33): 58 sweeps 327 down to 270 and 33 sweeps 252 down to 227, never crossing each other or 15's fixed 180, so the winding order at 16 survives the whole traverse. 39 moves now rather than later because at (33,42) it stays between 42 and 25 on row 42 with nothing in between.

Round 4 — step two of the 16 traverse along its locked row 40 (column 25 to 28). Nothing else moves: I keep each step of the traverse to three cells so that if a bearing at 16, 33, 15 or 58 does start to wind I lose one step rather than the whole slide. Row 40 is empty between columns 16 and 33, so the 15-16 horizontal simply lengthens and swallows nothing.

Round 5 — steps three and four of the 16 traverse, taken together now that the first two steps came back with an empty rejected list and confirmed the winding analysis holds along row 40. 16 lands on column 33, which is both 58's column and (after last round's nudge) 39's column, so this single placement closes two segments at once: 16-58 vertical over rows 33-40 and 16-39 vertical over rows 40-42. Both spans are empty of other vertices, and 15-16 stays horizontal because 16 never leaves row 40.
